claim: For every integer \(p\ge1\) and residue \(r\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\), let \(L_{p,r}=\{a^n:n\ge0,\ n\equiv r\pmod p\}\). The minimum number of states of a loop-free, epsilon-free NFA for \(L_{p,r}\) whose transitions all cross a fixed bipartition and whose underlying simple transition graph is a cactus equals \(\operatorname{lcm}(p,2)\); among unrestricted epsilon-free NFAs, which may have self-loops, the minimum is \(p\). Thus the structural constraint doubles the exact state minimum when \(p\) is odd and adds no states when \(p\) is even.

correctness.rationale: The lower bound follows from a simple directed cycle on an accepting run: its length must be divisible by \(p\) because all accepted lengths have residue \(r\), and must be even because every transition crosses the bipartition. Thus it is at least \(\operatorname{lcm}(p,2)\) states. The explicit cycle construction of that length recognizes exactly \(L_{p,r}\) and has a bipartite-cactus graph. The unrestricted \(p\)-cycle (allowing a self-loop when \(p=1\)) and matching cycle lower bound establish the baseline \(p\). Edge cases \(p=1\) and \(m=2\) are explicitly handled.

evidence: Grobler–Koziel–Siebertz, Theorem 1.1: every regular language has an epsilon-free NFA with bipartite-cactus transition graph.

value.rationale: The main paper explicitly leaves state-complexity bounds open. This theorem gives an exact and sharp infinite-family benchmark for that problem and quantifies the parity cost precisely: a factor of two for odd periods and no increase for even periods. The residue classes are canonical unary regular languages, so the result is a motivated structural boundary rather than an arbitrary finite example.
